title: How $100M Families Manage Money (Family Office CEO Explains)
guest: Holly MacDonald, incoming CEO (previously CIO and COO) of Bessemer Trust
summary: Holly MacDonald of Bessemer Trust explains what a family office does for ultra-high-net-worth families (average client about $100M) and how the same principles apply to anyone: start with the purpose of your wealth, automate saving like a bill, and hold a regular 'family office of one' review. She also shares career lessons on building a team rather than doing everything, 'fading' instead of quitting during overwhelming seasons, and using listening and good questions as a power move in male-dominated finance.

ideas.idea: A family office is a dedicated team handling all aspects of a family's financial life, and its real product is peace of mind and family well-being, not just growing wealth.
ideas.detail: Services span investment management, tax planning, estate planning and philanthropy. Bessemer's average client has around $100 million under management; the firm handles about $200B AUM.

ideas.idea: Being privately owned with only one line of business lets an advisor sit on the same side of the table as clients, avoiding the conflicts that come from pushing products.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: A public money manager's ultimate responsibility is to shareholders, so at some point goals conflict with clients; the hosts note many managers push their own funds and earn basis points on them, which undermines true fiduciary duty. Alignment lets the firm think clearly about how to help clients and pivot when needed.

ideas.idea: A CEO's differentiated skill is identifying people who can do what she can't and unleashing them, not doing everything herself.
ideas.detail: Trying to do everything yourself is a myth to bust for early-career people and would make you 'implode'. As COO she deliberately deepened in technology, operations and Gen AI processes, an area she wouldn't have listed as a top skill a few years ago.

ideas.idea: You can have it all, but not all at the same time: lean into career or family in different seasons rather than chasing perfect balance.
ideas.detail: Holly took a lateral-or-down career move to follow her husband to Brazil and had her twins there, prioritizing family; now, taking over as CEO early next year with 12-year-old twins, is her moment to lean into career.

ideas.idea: When life feels overwhelming, 'fade' a little rather than taking yourself out of the race entirely, because re-entry in finance is very hard.
ideas.detail: Finance has a high entry cost, so once you have a good role, hang in there even at less than 100%. Everyone fades whether they tell you or not; she recalls male colleagues who went to the golf store every lunch. She credits Dr. Laura Morgan Roberts' work on inclusivity for the idea of flexibility to fade.

ideas.idea: Skipping the networking event to rest, read or run does not hurt productivity; your best ideas come when you step away from the desk.
ideas.detail: She gets ideas for her team on morning runs with her dog; the hosts call it maximizing 'shower thoughts'. Jeff Bezos has said his most productive hour is walking around doing nothing in the morning. High achievers put too much pressure on themselves to give A+ every day.

ideas.idea: The most important starting question for any wealth is its purpose: preserve, grow, pass on, or give away, because that dictates structure, tax planning and asset allocation.
ideas.detail: Passing wealth to the next generation implies certain structuring; growing it for philanthropy implies a different allocation. If the purpose is the next generation, ask what values you want passed along too.

ideas.idea: About two-thirds of Bessemer's clients are first-generation wealth creators, and they want wealth to expand their children's choices, not give them an easy life.
ideas.detail: Inheritance can let a child be an entrepreneur or a social worker while keeping their desired lifestyle; the last thing a gritty founder wants is kids with no view on how the money was made.

ideas.idea: The most common goal is preservation, but pure preservation fails because inflation erodes wealth, so every family needs at least a strategy to maintain purchasing power.
ideas.detail: Whether the aim is big growth or just keeping up with inflation, some growth strategy is required.

ideas.idea: Family offices differ mainly in their long time horizon, which lets them hold illiquid assets like private equity and venture capital that early-career people can't afford to lock up.
ideas.detail: PE and VC return capital in 5-10+ years; someone unsure whether they'll need a house down payment in five years shouldn't over-allocate. Family offices can also chase bespoke one-off deals because they have a full team analyzing them. Bessemer has built ways for small pools (even a grandchild's account) to access top private-market managers.

ideas.idea: Anyone can run a 'mini family office' for themselves or with a partner: agree on the why, automate money movement toward savings, spending and giving, and review with regularity.
ideas.detail: Set automatic transfers into separate accounts or ledgers so you don't have to remember each paycheck. The hosts call it a 'family office of one'.

ideas.idea: Talking more openly about money, especially with a partner, raises the odds of meeting financial goals; money is becoming less taboo.
ideas.detail: Industry research and Bessemer's client experience show greater communication correlates with goal achievement and a positive experience. Start walking before running: open the conversation with parents gently rather than cornering them about inheritance.

ideas.idea: Most people never ask why they make money or where they want to be at 80, so put a calendar reminder to spend two hours once a year (or quarterly) answering those questions and setting goals.
ideas.detail: Treat savings like a bill you pay to yourself; it's not possible to think about this daily during wealth-creation mode, so create guardrails. Holly, a philosophy major, cites Socrates: 'the unexamined life is not worth living.'

ideas.idea: Holly is motivated by the intrinsic value of work and helping others succeed, with money as a measuring stick rather than the goal; she wouldn't move if she won the lottery.
ideas.detail: She values high-quality time with family over quantity and is fine with work travel as long as time at home is high value. She recommends Arthur Brooks' 'From Strength to Strength' for thinking about arcs and phases of life, and says priorities become clearer over time so don't be too hard on yourself early on.

ideas.idea: A liberal arts education teaches you how to think and analyze, and technical skills can be acquired later; a trendy CS major pursued without passion may be automated by AI.
ideas.detail: All three are liberal arts graduates who went into technical fields.

ideas.idea: In male-dominated finance, listening well and asking good questions is a power move: accumulate information over time, then act at the right moment.
ideas.detail: In a sales role covering mostly-male hedge fund managers, being female meant no macho ego competition, so she formed stronger relationships and heard what they really wanted. The hosts add 'information is power' and it only comes from active listening.

ideas.idea: When you disagree with someone, ask them a question ('how did you think about X?') instead of saying you disagree; you either learn something or they discover their own error without being called out.
ideas.detail: Learned from Bessemer's current CEO. Especially in big groups, questions rather than aggressive call-outs keep colleagues happier to work with you and build a team where people share ideas.

ideas.idea: Inclusive culture is not a warm fuzzy extra; it's where the best ideas come from, often from the person who joined two months ago rather than the 30-year veteran.
ideas.detail: One mean comment in a group meeting can set an open culture back months. Junior people should thoughtfully step into gaps even senior people miss. The hosts argue this openness to input is why women are better investors. Bessemer's executive committee is at least half female.

ideas.idea: Trust your first instinct because it reflects subconscious processing of information, but where you can afford to, give yourself time before acting on it.
ideas.detail: Jean says she has moved from over-analyzing to trusting her first instinct after repeatedly finding it was right; Cherie always feels the gut signal but tends to rationalize it away.

ideas.idea: The most outrageous things done in the name of love can be self-love, like ending an eight-year engagement, or adventure, like moving to Brazil without speaking Portuguese.
ideas.detail: Jean ended her eight-year relationship/engagement for self-love; Cherie jumped too fast into a relationship during COVID; Holly moved to Brazil for her husband and adopted a puppy rescued from Ukraine's front lines via Sochi Dogs.
